- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) in recent history, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly to align with bullish momentum.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and price is trending down, model often overcorrects downward — avoid sharp drops; allow slight upward bias.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots — cap forecast growth to 5–7% above prior peak.  
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline after peak), model often fails to recognize — reduce forecast slope slightly.  
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly while true outcome shows accelerating upward trend, model underestimates momentum — increase forecast slope by 1–2% per day.  
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early days (first 5–7) — adjust downward by 1–2% for days 1–5 if sentiment is neutral or negative.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 values, model tends to be overly conservative — allow 1–2% upward bias in forecast to capture latent volatility.  
- When true outcome exceeds model forecast by >10% in first 3–5 days, model is lagging — adjust forecast upward by 1–3% for next 3–5 days to catch momentum.
